lead: A name is a handle people use; an address is where the thing sits. Naming resolves the first into the second, step by step. A distributed file system uses naming so a file on a remote server opens like a local path, then decides where to cache bytes and when a write becomes visible. NFS, AFS and HDFS all make this trade. Only a few universities teach this chapter, so keep the mechanism clear.
prereq: You need Unit 4 for remote procedure call and message cost, and Unit 5 for consistency models.

sections.h3: From names to addresses, flat and structured

blocks.text: A name is a string such as notes.txt. An identifier names at most one entity, such as an inode number. An address is where the entity is reached, such as server S plus a file handle. Resolution maps a name to an address. A flat name has no structure, so the system needs a search rule.

items: Broadcast asks every server; message cost grows with server count.
Forwarding pointer stays at the old address; long chains add lookups.
Home-based naming keeps one home address; the home becomes a hotspot.
DHT hashes the name to a key and stores the key on the node that owns it.

blocks.text: owner(k) = first node clockwise from h(k)
blocks.where: k is the key from the name; h(k) is its position on a 2^m ring of m bits; owner(k) is the node that stores k. Consistent hashing moves few keys when a node joins or leaves.

blocks.text: A structured name is a path such as /home/ravi/notes.txt. The name space is a labelled graph: directories are internal nodes, files are leaves, edges carry component names. Resolution walks one component at a time; each component returns the next node. An absolute name starts at the root; a relative name starts at the current directory.

A mount point is a local directory where a remote export is spliced in. /home/ravi/remote can represent server S's /export/ravi. The closure is the set of nodes visited. A hard link is another name for the same identifier; a soft link stores a path and breaks if the target moves.

sections.h3: Distributed file systems: caching and freshness

blocks.text: A distributed file system has two access models. In the remote access model, each read or write goes to the server and the client keeps no local copy. In the upload/download model, the client downloads the whole file, works locally, and uploads it changed.

Caching can hold a whole file or fixed-size blocks. The cache can sit on the client disk, in client memory, or in server memory. Client disk survives a crash but is slower; client memory is faster but lost on reboot; server memory helps repeated reads.
Sharing semantics decide when a write becomes visible.

items: Unix semantics: a read after a write sees the write immediately, even from another client.
Session semantics: changes become visible when the file is closed.
Immutable files: a file never changes; a new version gets a new name.
Transaction semantics: reads and writes appear atomic, as in a database transaction.

blocks.text: NFS v3 uses a stateless server: it keeps no per-client open or lock state, and every operation is idempotent, so a retry after a lost reply is safe. NFS resolves one path component per RPC and caches a file handle per component. AFS caches whole files on client disks and validates them on open. HDFS stores fixed-size blocks and keeps block locations in a single NameNode.

figure.caption: The directory remote is a mount point. notes.txt looks local under /home/ravi, but its file handle lives on server S.

spec.aria: A local naming tree where remote is a mount point that splices server S's exported directory under ravi, so notes.txt looks local but is stored on S.

examples.question: A client opens /home/ravi/remote/notes.txt. The directory /home/ravi/remote is a mount point for the export /export/ravi on server S. (a) List the lookups and say which go to S. (b) How many round trips to S are needed on the first open, and on the second open of the same file if the client caches the file handles of remote and notes.txt?
steps: 1. Resolve /, home, ravi locally: 3 local lookups.
2. remote is a mount point for S:/export/ravi; use its cached handle or one RPC if absent.
3. Ask S for notes.txt inside /export/ravi: 1 RPC to S, which returns its file handle.
4. First open: 1 round trip to S.
5. Second open with both handles cached and the file unchanged: 0 round trips to S.
6. Closure = {/, home, ravi, S:/export/ravi, S:/export/ravi/notes.txt}; size 5.
examples.answer: First open: 1 round trip to S; second open: 0 round trips; closure size: 5.
examples.check:
local_lookups=3
remote_rpcs=1
first=remote_rpcs
second=0
closure=5
print(local_lookups)
print(remote_rpcs)
print(first)
print(second)
print(closure)

traps: A mount point is a local directory, not the remote root. The remote root here is /export/ravi.
NFS v3 keeps no per-client state; a retry must repeat safely, so operations are idempotent.
Whole-file caching fetches the full file; block caching fetches only needed blocks. Do not mix them.
Unix semantics makes a write visible immediately; session semantics waits for close.
A hard link names the same identifier; a soft link stores a path.

quiz.a: A name is a string. An identifier names at most one entity. An address is where the entity is reached.

quiz.q: Why does consistent hashing move few keys when a node joins?
quiz.a: Only keys between the new node and its predecessor change owner; other ring positions stay put.

quiz.q: A 16-slot ring has nodes at 2 and 9. h(k)=13. Which node owns k?
quiz.a: Walk clockwise from 13: the next node is 2, so node 2 owns k.

quiz.q: An NFS v3 reply is lost after a successful write. Why is a client retry safe?
quiz.a: The server is stateless and the write is idempotent, so repeating it gives the same server state.

quiz.q: Compare remote access and upload/download models.
quiz.a: Remote access sends each operation to the server. Upload/download moves the whole file to the client and back.

quiz.q: Two clients share a file. When does the second client see the first client's write under Unix and session semantics?
quiz.a: Unix semantics: immediately after the write. Session semantics: when the first client closes the file.

quiz.q: What does the HDFS NameNode hold?
quiz.a: It holds the block locations for files; data blocks sit on DataNodes.

beyond: Not for the exam. NFS v4 adds state, sessions and stronger security; SMB is its main rival. Object stores replace paths with flat keys and HTTP, and HDFS-style systems split metadata from blocks. Search terms: NFSv4, AFS callbacks, HDFS NameNode, object storage consistency, close-to-open consistency.
